I'm still a redditor, for now.

What keeps me there is the hope that it'll be the open, crowdsourced communication platform of the future. It really should be. There's no excuse not to take that spot. Specifically, what led me down this route was:

  • Crowdsourced, Open Discussions. StackOverflow forced me to reddit, unwillingly. StackOverflow as a Q&A resource is crowdsourced like reddit, but became too limiting with its no-discussions rules and single-answer, one-time format per post. Except for post-locking based on date, reddit allows me to look up anything with real-world users that actually have some meaningful experience based on shared interests or events. It still does this, and I actually love it during big purchase decisions (surfboards, when I bought my new phone... or any digital hardware, really, D&D versions and their merits, Heroes of the Storm skins screenshots and complaints, etc.).
  • Flexibility. There's a huge power at the multi-user and single-user scope, even with its features today. My own subreddits include http://reddit.com/r/realnosleep (I didn't like the direction nosleep went; I could make my own!) and http://reddit.com/r/softwarebacklog (my place to put in all my complaints about any software, experimenting with the replacement of feature/bug databases so that end users can have input on development/priority through votes).
  • Drama. There is no better insight into both real and first-world problems than the multitude of subreddits that pop up to track, discuss, or offensively insult them. Reddit's core value proposition includes the ability to be both the dynamic content distribution system and the higher-level, meta management system that observes it.

The openness made for a beautiful communication and distribution wherein all the good and bad could be observed at multiple levels -- and even so, I would say that reddit still hasn't been used to its full potential. I'm excited to see more platforms offer this potential.

Charges implies it wasn't verified or proven. The Harvard Jewish quota is now a matter of undisputed fact. It's actually because of this quota that schools like Harvard openly no longer recruit based just on merit. You don't have to look hard to find the stories of the ostensibly perfect students being turned away. The euphemism used for this is character based recruitment.

But it wasn't always this way. In the early 20th century and earlier there was no "character based recruitment." Harvard had an entrance exam - if you passed it, you were in. Here is one such exam from 1869. The reason they had to institute a quota instead of simply rejecting otherwise perfectly acceptable students is that admission used to be entirely meritocratic, and too many individuals they considered undesirable (in the 20s following World War 1 Jews were mostly part of a largely disenfranchised lower class) were becoming meritorious. The quota was eventually done away with, but in its place came this system of "character based recruitment" that effectively enables quotas and all other sorts of nastiness, but allows them to do it more opaquely.

People are certainly well aware of the no-name "perfect" applicants being rejected. And they're certainly also aware of the politician or CEO's bumbling son being accepted. But they might not realize the magnitude. At Harvard now a days more than 45% of their students come from families in the top 3.8% of earners.
